newsitem.title: CHINA: China-ruled Hong Kong reveals election laws.
newsitem.headline: China-ruled Hong Kong reveals election laws.

text.p: The China-backed Hong Kong government on Friday published a new election law that will curtail democracy in the former British colony, provoking condemnation from pro-democracy activists.

Revealing the draft election law for the first time, Constitutional Affairs Secretary Michael Suen said the public should not be "petty-minded" over the issue of only one-third of the 60 seats legislature to be returned by geographical constituencies in next May's polls.

The remaining 40 seats will be filled by representatives from business and professional bodies in so-called functional constituencies, and by an election committee made up of pro-China politicians, businessmen and professionals.

"Whatever else regarding the election committee, the functional constituencies, I do look upon them as expedience, transient arrangements which will not last," Suen told a news conference. "Our main focus should be on direct election."
Suen said the government would present the draft law to the China-anointed provisional legislature next Wednesday, hoping it would be passed by the end of September.

Under the new arrangements, more than two million people who were eligible to vote in the 1995 Legislative Council polls' functional constituencies would be disenfranchised. They would be replaced by corporate votes adding up to no more than 200,000 ballots.
The pro-democracy movement in the territory blasted the plan.

"The majority of the seats in the Legislative Council will be dominated by the rich and the powerful, and the pro-Communists, so this system is fraudulent, undemocratic and bad. It should be exposed and condemned," ousted pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau told reporters.

Lau, along with the members of the territory's popular Democratic Party, were thrown out of office on July 1 when China took over Hong Kong from the British, ending 156 years of colonial rule. They were replaced by members of the provisional legislature.

The Democratic Party also blasted the new law. "This... arrangement is designed for those who Mr Tung wants to see to be elected," said ousted Democratic Party legislator Lee Wing-tat, referring to Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa.

Britain's chief diplomat in Hong Kong, Francis Cornish, welcomed the government's plan to hold the election as early as May, but voiced misgiving about the rollback of democracy in the changes to the functional constituency system.
In 1995, 2.7 million Hong Kong people had the right to vote in those constituencies, but under the post-colonial system only 200,000 will be allowed to vote, Cornish told Reuters.
